sourceLines.text: Subject Introduction
What is Social Studies?

Social studies is the study of history, geography, economics, civics and citizenship, and government and politics. Students explore important questions and actively engage with issues to understand lessons from the past and to become active and well-

informed citizens in their communities. Students use a knowledge-based curriculum and combine social science methods, including research, source evaluation, and evidence interpretation, to enhance understanding, draw conclusions, and build robust
critical-thinking skills.
History

Social studies gives students a strong understanding of local, national, and international history. By understanding the past, students can interpret the present. By learning about societies, cultures, and civilizations, students will be equipped to
understand the origins of current events and the roles of institutions.
Supporting Active and Responsible Citizens

Social studies empowers students to become active and responsible citizens by developing their critical-thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making skills. Students learn about the importance of rights and responsibilities and will understand the
various ways in which citizens can and should participate in their communities.
Critical Thinking

Social studies equips students with essential critical-thinking skills by encouraging them to question assumptions, ask questions, consider bias, and build resilience in a rapidly changing world. Historical, comparative, quantitative, and political analysis

improves students’ understanding of perspectives, bias, motivations, and actions from the past and supports students’ decision making in the present and future. Students also develop an understanding of research methods and learn to practise

objective and impartial inquiry, investigation, and analysis of primary and secondary sources. These skills support students’ understanding of the significance of historical events, which will inform lifelong critical thinking.

Critical thinking in social studies involves more than memorization and recall. Critical thinking is reinforced through students’ engagement with developmentally appropriate sources, content, resources, and learning experiences and contributes to

students’ literacy and numeracy development. The skills and procedures in Alberta’s social studies curriculum require students to interpret evidence, determine significance, recognize perspectives, analyze patterns and relationships, and consider ethics.
The study and creation of primary and secondary sources is essential to understanding complex historical and contemporary issues.

Students develop their critical-thinking skills when they listen to, read, and view a variety of primary and secondary sources and they demonstrate their critical-thinking skills when they speak, write, and represent to express their evidence-based

viewpoints. When students communicate their ideas through debates, discussions, presentations, research reports, opinion pieces, and structured writing, they develop higher-order thinking skills and the ability to contribute to dialogue and discussion.
Media Literacy

Media literacy is a crucial skill for interacting with complex and sometimes conflicting information from a variety of sources. Media literacy is an essential component of critical thinking and serves as a bridge to real-world experiences. In social studies,

students develop and practise media literacy skills, including digital literacy skills, when they access and engage effectively with historical and contemporary issues, which helps them analyze information, communicate ideas, and participate as informed
citizens.
Supporting Career and Academic Pathways

Alberta students have diverse career and academic goals. These goals are supported in social studies by developing Alberta’s eight core competencies: critical thinking, problem solving, research and managing information, creativity and innovation,

communication, citizenship, collaboration, and personal growth and well-being. Engaging in these various levels of thinking, from foundational understanding to complex analysis and evaluation, prepares Alberta students for real-world experiences, for
successful and fulfilling lives, and to make meaningful contributions in their communities and the world.

Engaging students in interpreting evidence, determining significance, recognizing perspectives, analyzing patterns and relationships, and considering ethics develops transferable skills that support the pursuit of a variety of career and academic interests.

When addressing historical and contemporary issues, educators, parents, and caregivers support engagement with social studies through approaches that are both developmentally appropriate and essential preparation for many career and academic
pursuits. The selection of age-appropriate content, resources, and real-world learning experiences can include:

• listening, reading, and viewing a variety of primary and secondary sources, texts such as lectures, discussions, oral histories, speeches, interviews, historical documents, biographies, articles, editorials, books, maps, charts, political cartoons, news
clips, films, documentaries, photographs, artwork, artifacts, performances, and other media texts; and

• speaking, writing, and representing using a variety of forms to communicate ideas, such as informal and formal debates, discussions, presentations, research reports, structured writing, opinion pieces, and other texts to inform and/or persuade.
Social Studies in Our World

Social studies promotes engaged and critically informed, active citizens. Globally, citizenship is dynamic, contextual, and multi-dimensional. Definitions of citizenship and its key features change across time and place based on the application and

interpretation of values. Active citizenship involves a range of practices that ultimately seek to help people be active participants in their world. Social studies acknowledges that students bring their own perspectives, cultures, and experiences to the
evolving world around them.

Students connect prior knowledge with new contexts to construct learning in ways that enrich their evolving understanding. Students recognize that diverse cultures, histories, contributions, and perspectives support a pluralistic society. Social studies

provides opportunities for the exploration of historical, contemporary, and emerging issues through the lens of multiple perspectives. The opportunity to respectfully debate, discuss, and address ethical questions prepares students for their future.

Engaging respectfully with multiple perspectives, including those of First Nations, Métis, Inuit, and Francophone communities, contributes to a deeper understanding of the worldviews that shape how individuals and groups interact in the world.

Organizing Idea Time and Place: Exploring the dynamic relationships between people, place, and time supports understanding of perspectives and events to make meaning of the world.
Guiding Question How can urbanization shift and shape a society?
Learning Outcome Students examine the impacts of urbanization and the growth of industry on Canada.
Knowledge
Patterns of immigration can be identified as push and pull factors that
motivate people to migrate from one place to another.
Canada experienced changing and increasingly urbanized demographics
due to international migration after the Second World War and urban centres
reflected a more diverse, pluralistic population.
Displaced persons are refugees, including Holocaust survivors, who
migrated to Canada following the Second World War (1945–51).
Urbanization and population boom after the Second World War increased
consumption and demand for development.
Urbanization influenced the growth and transformation of industries and the
emergence of new sectors in Canada, including
• public infrastructure development to support growth of suburbs and
population
• oil and gas exploration, and the growth of the petroleum industry
• hydroelectricity production
• automobile and paper production
There are environmental impacts of urbanization, such as
• pollution
• land consumption
• land division
• wildlife migration changes
Understanding
Urbanization impacts a country’s population, economy, and environment.
Skills & Procedures
Relate patterns of immigration to push and pull factors.
Explain changes to Canada’s demographics after the Second World War.
Explain social, economic, and environmental consequences and challenges
of increased urbanization.
Investigate how new fields are responding to urbanization.
Evaluate the impacts of the growth of oil and gas industry in Canada.
Consider the benefits of the growth of Canada’s petroleum industry.
Organizing Idea Time and Place: Exploring the dynamic relationships between people, place, and time supports understanding of perspectives and events to make meaning of the world.
Guiding Question How did Canada become a more independent nation and expand democratic rights?
Learning Outcome Students explain how Canada gained independence and expanded democratic rights.
Knowledge
Canada’s increasing autonomy, including the 1926 Balfour Declaration and
the 1931 Statute of Westminster, represented the formal transition of Canada
from a self-governing colony to a fully sovereign nation.
Canada gained full authority over its own foreign policy.
The shift from a centralized empire to a commonwealth of independent
nations was driven by a combination of post-war exhaustion, intense
diplomatic pressure from the Dominions, and a pragmatic desire to maintain
influence through cooperation rather than coercion.
Women’s suffrage in Canada was the decades-long movement to secure the
right of women to vote and hold political office.
The Famous Five were a group of five prominent Alberta women who
launched a legal challenge that fundamentally redefined the status of women
in Canadian law.
By establishing that women were legal persons, the Persons Case affirmed
that women had the right to hold any appointed or elected office in the
country, reinforcing the democratic principle of equality.
Understanding
Canada became a sovereign nation and its identity evolved as more people
gained rights.
Skills & Procedures
Analyze how the Balfour Declaration (1926) and the Statute of Westminster
(1931) transformed Canada’s political independence.
Explain how gaining control over foreign policy contributed to Canada’s
development as a sovereign nation.
Explain how the Famous Five case changed the distribution of political power
and participation in Canada.
Compare how political independence and expanded rights contributed to
changes in Canadian identity.
Organizing Idea Time and Place: Exploring the dynamic relationships between people, place, and time supports understanding of perspectives and events to make meaning of the world.
Guiding Question How did WWII shape Canada’s independence?
Learning Outcome Students examine how Canada’s identity was shaped by its independent role in WWII and its growing global influence.
Knowledge
Canada’s Parliament declared war independently in 1939 and entered the
Second World War, which represented a significant step forward in its
sovereignty and identity.
Canada’s independent participation in WWII contributed to its emergence as
a self-governing nation with a distinct international role.
More than one million Canadians joined the armed forces, allowing the
country to build one of the world’s largest navies and air forces by 1945.
Canadian forces earned recognition on the battlefield and were highly
regarded. They made important contributions during the
• Defence of Hong Kong (1941)
• Dieppe Raid (1942)
• Italian Campaign (1943)
• D-Day and the Battle of Normandy (1944)
• Liberation of France, Belgium and the Netherlands (1944-45)
Canada’s diverse populations and communities, such as Chinese Canadians
in Force 136, made contributions to the Second World War.
Cree code talkers were First Nations and Métis soldiers who developed and
contributed a military coding system based on the Cree language, which was
invaluable to communications during the Second World War.
The Second World War transformed Canada into a more prominent
international actor, strengthening its global reputation and influence.
Understanding
Canada’s identity was shaped by its independent role in WWII and its
growing global influence.
Skills & Procedures
Analyze how Canada’s decision to declare war independently in 1939
demonstrated its growing sovereignty.
Explain how participation in WWII contributed to Canada’s development as a
self-governing nation.
Use evidence from battles (e.g., Hong Kong, Dieppe, Italy, D-Day, liberation
of Europe) to explain Canada’s contributions to Allied success.
Explain the significance of contributions by groups such as Chinese
Canadians and Cree code talkers to the war effort.
Evaluate the extent to which the Second World War was a turning point in
Canada’s development as an independent and influential nation.
Organizing Idea Time and Place: Exploring the dynamic relationships between people, place, and time supports understanding of perspectives and events to make meaning of the world.
Guiding Question How did political, economic, and social changes reshape Canada after WWII?
Learning Outcome Students analyze how post-war developments shaped Canada as a modern nation.
Knowledge
After World War II, Canada developed into a welfare state, where the
government expanded social programs, including universal healthcare and
old-age pensions, to reduce inequality and provide financial security.
The welfare state emerged in response to the economic hardships of the
Great Depression, as well as wartime experiences that increased
expectations for government support.
After WWII, Canada played an active role in promoting global peace and
security, strengthening its identity as a cooperative and responsible
international partner.
Canada became a founding member of NATO, contributing to collective
defence during the Cold War.
Canada participated in the Korean War, including key battles such as
Kapyong and Hill 355, demonstrating its military commitment to global
stability.
Canada worked with the United States through NORAD to defend North
America from external threats.
Canada helped resolve international conflicts, including the Suez Crisis,
where Lester B. Pearson’s leadership contributed to the creation of modern
peacekeeping and earned him the Nobel Peace Prize.
Canada’s continued involvement in peacekeeping missions around the world
strengthened its reputation as a nation committed to diplomacy and global
cooperation.
After WWII, immigration patterns shifted, with increasing numbers of
immigrants arriving from non-European regions such as India, China, and
Vietnam.
Displaced persons are refugees, including Holocaust survivors, who
migrated to Canada following the Second World War (1945-51).
These new waves of immigration contributed to Canada’s growing cultural
diversity and reshaped its population and identity.
The development of multiculturalism reflected efforts to recognize and
include diverse cultural groups within Canadian society.
Government policies such as Residential Schools and the Sixties Scoop
caused long-term harm to Indigenous communities by separating children
from their families and cultures.
Canadian identity has been shaped by internal disagreements and
challenges to national unity.
Events such as the October Crisis (1970) and debates surrounding Quebec
separatism reflect differing views about Canada’s political and cultural future.
The Meech Lake Accord (1987) attempted to address Quebec’s status within
Canada but revealed ongoing tensions between regions.
The growth of the petroleum industry contributed to economic prosperity,
particularly in Western Canada.
Government policies such as the National Energy Program aimed to manage
energy resources but led to conflict between regions.
These tensions contributed to Western alienation, where Western
Canadians, particularly those in Alberta and Saskatchewan, felt
underrepresented or disadvantaged by federal decisions.
The Constitution Act (1982) was a major milestone in Canadian
independence, as Canada gained full control over its own constitution.
The inclusion of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms strengthened
protections for individual rights and freedoms.
This marked a significant step in shaping Canada’s identity as a nation
based on democracy, equality, and the rule of law.
Understanding
Canada’s identity evolved after the Second World War through change,
cooperation, and conflict.
Skills & Procedures
Evaluate the impact of social programs (e.g., healthcare, pensions) on
reducing inequality and shaping Canadian society.
Evaluate how Canada’s international actions (e.g., NATO, Korean War,
peacekeeping) influenced both its global reputation and national identity.
Assess how the development of multiculturalism shaped Canadian identity.
Analyze the impact of Residential Schools and the Sixties Scoop on
Indigenous communities.
Analyze how events such as the October Crisis and Quebec separatism
reflected differing views of Canadian identity.
Analyze the impact of the petroleum industry on economic development and
regional identity.
Assess the causes and consequences of Western alienation.
Evaluate the extent to which post-war developments strengthened or
challenged Canadian identity.
Evaluate how the Constitution Act (1982) and the Charter of Rights and
Freedoms transformed Canadian identity and participation in society.
Organizing Idea Systems: Evaluating processes and structures of organizations builds understanding of decision making in the world.
Guiding Question How did economic changes transform Canada into a modern economy?
Learning Outcome Students analyze how economic crisis, growth, and global trade shaped Canada’s modern economy.
Knowledge
The Great Depression (1930s) was a period of severe economic hardship
marked by high unemployment, falling prices, and widespread poverty.
The Great Depression was caused by several factors, including
• overproduction of goods
• declining consumer demand
• the collapse of global trade
• financial instability
In response to the Great Depression, governments in Canada and the United
States began to take a more active role in the economy such as public
works, social welfare programs, and deficit spending.
After World War II, Canada’s economy expanded and diversified, contributing
to the development of a modern industrial economy. This included the growth
of economic sectors including
• automobile manufacturing
• petroleum and energy production
• papers and forestry
• hydroelectric power development
Canada’s population became increasingly urbanized after WWII, with more
people living in cities rather than rural areas.
The growth of suburbs occurred as people moved to residential areas
outside city centres in search of affordable housing and improved living
conditions.
Canada developed an increasingly close trade relationship with the United
States, reflecting geographic proximity and economic interdependence.
Agreements such as NAFTA expanded free trade, increasing the movement
of goods, services, and investment between the two countries.
Understanding
Canada’s economy evolved through crisis, government action, and global
trade.
Skills & Procedures
Analyze the causes of the Great Depression and their impact on economic
stability.
Analyze how governments responded to economic crises through policies
such as public works, social programs, and deficit spending.
Analyze how Canada’s economy transformed after WWII through industrial
growth and the emergence of new sectors.
Analyze how economic growth contributed to urbanization and the
development of suburban communities.
Evaluate the social and economic consequences of increased urbanization.
Analyze how Canada’s trade relationship with the United States shaped its
economic development.
Evaluate the impact of free trade agreements on economic growth and
interdependence.
Evaluate the extent to which economic developments contributed to Canada
becoming a modern, industrial, and globally connected nation.
Organizing Idea Systems: Evaluating processes and structures of organizations builds understanding of decision making in the world.
Guiding Question How is power organized and exercised in Canada’s system of government?
Learning Outcome Students analyze how power is distributed and exercised in Canada’s government, including how laws are made and how rights are protected.
Knowledge
Responsible government is a principle of Canada’s parliamentary democracy
in which the executive branch must maintain the confidence of the elected
House of Commons to remain in power.
Responsible government means that the government is accountable to
elected representatives, who act on behalf of citizens.
If the government loses the support of the House of Commons, it must resign
or call an election. Canada’s Parliament consists of three parts: the Crown,
the Senate, and the House of Commons, which must all approve laws.
The Crown is represented by the Governor General which represent the
Monarch and gives Royal Assent to laws.
The House of Commons is comprised of elected representatives, Members
of Parliament, who represent a riding. They are responsible for making new
laws through debate and voting.
A riding (also called a constituency or electoral district) is a geographic area
in Canada that elects one Member of Parliament (MP) to represent it in the
House of Commons.
The Senate consists of appointed members who review laws passed by the
House of Commons.
Laws are created through a formal legislative process, including
• bill drafting
• first reading (introduction)
• second reading (debate)
• committee stage (detailed review)
• third reading (final approval)
• approval by the Senate
• royal assent by the Crown
A formal legislative process ensures that laws are debated, reviewed, and
approved by multiple institutions before being enacted.
Governments also make decisions through:
• Orders in Council
• Regulations and Directives
• Ministerial Orders/Decisions
Canada is a federal system, meaning power is divided between federal and
provincial governments.
The Federal government is responsible for
• Defence
• Banking and Currency
• Trade and Commerce
• Criminal Law
• Citizenship
Provincial governments are responsible for
• Education
• Healthcare
• Property and Civil Rights
• Municipalities
• Natural Resources
Provinces have primary authority over natural resources, including their
development, management, and use.
Jurisdiction over natural resources is critical to Alberta because
• its economy relies heavily on oil and gas development
• it controls resource revenues (e.g., royalties)
• it shapes decisions about economic growth and development
Conflicts can arise between federal and provincial governments when
resource issues involve national interests such as the environment or
interprovincial trade.
Canada’s judiciary (court system) interprets and applies the law, ensuring
laws follow the Constitution.
Lower courts establish the facts of a case and make the initial decision.
Appeal courts ensure that laws are applied correctly and consistently.
The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest and final court in the country.
The Supreme Court ensures that laws are interpreted consistently across
Canada and that they follow the Constitution.
The Canadian Citizenship Act (1947) formally established Canadian
citizenship and defined membership in the nation.
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982) protects fundamental
rights such as
• freedom of expression
• equality
• legal protections
Canadian citizens have rights (e.g., voting, freedoms) and responsibilities,
including
• obeying laws
• participating in democracy
• respecting the rights of others
Understanding
Power in Canada is shared and exercised through democratic structures,
laws, and institutions, which shape decision making, protect rights, and
ensure accountability.
Skills & Procedures
Examine how power is distributed between federal and provincial
governments and how this shapes decision making in Canada.
Assess how responsible government ensures accountability in Canada’s
political system.
Explain how representation through ridings connects citizens to government
decision making.
Interpret how government tools (e.g., regulations, orders in council) shape
decisions beyond Parliament.
Explain how the judiciary interprets laws and places limits on government
authority.
Examine how the Charter of Rights and Freedoms influences laws and
government actions.
Investigate how control over natural resources shapes provincial decision
making and regional perspectives.
Connect how Canada’s system of government balances power,
accountability, and rights.
Formulate a judgement on how fairly power is distributed among
governments and citizens in Canada.
Organizing Idea Citizenship: Understanding local, national, and global issues empowers individual and collective action toward an inclusive society.
Guiding Question In what ways do citizen rights evolve?
Learning Outcome Students examine the impact of changing legislation on citizenship in Canada.
Knowledge
Canada is a democratic nation that balances government control and
protection of citizens’ individual rights and freedoms.
Canada’s government policies and programs reflect changing perspectives
and impact individuals and groups in different ways.
Changes in legislation extended individual rights that were once denied to
people based on
• age
• race
• gender
• income
• ethnic origin
• religious or spiritual beliefs
Individuals and groups have changed the social and political landscape in
Canada through advocacy for changes in legislation, including advocacy for
women’s suffrage by the Famous Five.
Prior to the Canadian Citizenship Act (1947), citizens in Canada were
considered British subjects.
The Canadian Citizenship Act (1947) defined who could hold or obtain
Canadian citizenship and was in response to increased international
recognition and the increasingly diverse population of Canada after the
Second World War.
Legislation has been amended over time to reflect Canadian pluralism and
immigration from non-European countries, such as India, China, the
Philippines, and Vietnam, including
• the ability to pass on citizenship from one generation to the next
• inclusive point systems and designations, such as economic, family,
refugee, and humanitarian classes
In Canada, citizenship status can be designated as
• citizen at birth or through naturalization
• temporary resident with a study, work, or visitor permit
• permanent resident
• refugee
Permanent residents and refugees in Canada are non-citizens with some of
the same rights as citizens and some restrictions.
The Canadian Bill of Rights (1960) was the first federal legislation outlining

Canada’s federal government further advanced rights by creating
commissions and legislation that helped the development of Canadian
multiculturalism and immigration, for example,
• the Royal Commission of Bilingualism and Biculturalism (1963)
• the Royal Commission on the Status of Women (1967)
• the Official Languages Act (1969)
• the Canadian Multiculturalism Policy (1971)
Canada gained sovereign control over its constitution through gradual
patriation, culminating in the Constitution Act (1982), which entrenched the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms (1982) defines individual and
collective rights, including
• fundamental freedoms
• democratic rights
• mobility rights
• legal rights
• equality rights
• official language rights
• minority language educational rights
• Canada’s multicultural heritage
• Indigenous peoples’ rights
Section 1 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms recognizes that
reasonable limits may be placed on rights and freedoms, including
censorship of hate speech e.g., racism, antisemitism, or Islamophobia.
Changes to the Constitution Act and the Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms can be made through
• the amending formula that allows the federal government to make additions
• the notwithstanding clause that allows provincial governments to exempt
certain sections
Attempts to amend the Constitution of Canada to encourage national unity
include
• the 1987 Meech Lake Accord
• the Charlottetown Accord
Rights afforded to Canadian citizens come with responsibilities of
• obeying the law
• taking responsibility for oneself and one’s family
• serving on a jury
• voting in elections
• helping others in the community
• protecting Canadian identity and the environment
Understanding
Protection of individual and collective rights evolves based on societal
change.

freedoms since Confederation.
